## Key Milestones and Catalysts

Nittobo's most important disclosed catalysts through the frozen date clustered in four documents rather than in a long stream of promotional releases. The first was the FY2024-2027 medium-term plan, which reorganized the group into five business divisions and set the original four-year capital-investment envelope at approximately ¥80 billion. [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm)

The second was the August 2025 capacity decision in Fukushima. Nittobo's integrated report said the company decided in August 2025 to expand glass fiber cloth production at the Fukushima Enterprise Center, and METI's 7 August 2025 approval summary laid out the scale of the related supply-security plan for low-thermal-expansion glass cloth for advanced logic ICs. [Integrated Report 2025](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/pdf/Nittobo_Integrated-Report_2025.pdf), [METI approval summary](https://www.meti.go.jp/policy/economy/economic_security/semicon/nintei_anpohandoutai_keikaku_27.pdf)

The third was the management transition effective 1 April 2026, when Hisanobu Hayashi was listed as Representative and Chief Executive Officer and Hiroyuki Tada as Director and Deputy Chairman. [Directors and officers](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/sustainability/governance/executive.html)

The fourth was the 12 May 2026 full-year release. That filing not only reported ¥118.229 billion of sales and ¥20.819 billion of operating profit for the year ended 31 March 2026; it also guided to ¥137 billion and ¥26 billion for the following year and, in the accompanying presentation, lifted FY2027 medium-term targets to ¥155 billion of sales and ¥36 billion of operating profit. [FY2026 financial results](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym2/202884/00.pdf), [FY2026 results presentation](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym3/202886/00.pdf)

A more tactical but still revealing catalyst sat between the Fukushima decision and the May 2026 result. In October 2025 Nittobo Taiwan announced it would exhibit low-CTE glass, low-DK glass and ultra-thin glass cloth at TPCA Show Taipei 2025, a reminder that the company was not merely expanding supply but also marketing the next-generation product set into the PCB industry that consumed it. [TPCA Show Taipei 2025 release](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/news/pdf/20251008_newsrelease.pdf)

chapters.title: Glass fiber technology IP, low-Dk innovation, R&D framework
chapters.body:
## The Chemistry of Competitive Advantage, in the Company's Own Disclosures

The cleanest primary-source correction to the old R&D chapter is that Nittobo's public materials were much more specific on measurable properties than on confidential formulations. The NE-glass page said the product lowered alkaline-earth content relative to general-purpose E-glass and raised boric-acid content, producing a 1 GHz dielectric constant of 4.8 and a dielectric dissipation factor of 0.0015, versus 6.8 and 0.0035 for E-glass. [NE-glass](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/business/electronicmaterials/ne-glass.htm)

The T-glass page gave the corresponding mechanical and thermal case: higher silica and alumina content, tensile strength of 4.8 GPa, tensile elasticity modulus of 86 GPa and a thermal expansion coefficient of 2.8 x10^-6/°C, versus 3.2 GPa, 75 GPa and 5.6 for E-glass. The integrated report then linked those disclosed properties to actual end uses in semiconductor package substrates. [T-glass](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/business/electronicmaterials/t-glass.htm), [Integrated Report 2025](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/pdf/Nittobo_Integrated-Report_2025.pdf)

## R&D Organisation

The current medium-term plan said the Research & Development Headquarters, established in 2017, was reorganized effective 1 April 2024. Product development functions were pushed into each business division, while the Technology Development Division was left responsible for company-wide product development functions, basic research and production technology. The business-locations page separately put the Technology Development Division at the Fukuyama Enterprise Center in Koriyama, Fukushima Prefecture. [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm), [Business locations](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/corporate/location/index.htm)

That formal reorganisation corrected an important point in the earlier dossier. The public structure by the frozen date was not a single monolithic central laboratory owning all R&D; it was a hybrid of division-led development and a company-wide technology function designed to shorten the route from materials science to production.

The plan also set out three policy pillars for the Technology Development Division. The first was what the company called ambidextrous development: deepening knowledge by innovating production and technology foundations while also exploring new markets by redefining core technology. The second was open innovation with outside partners. The third was digital innovation, including the use of MI and AI to improve development and process work. [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm)

The product pages added enough hard data to show that these were not rhetorical categories. T-glass was disclosed with SiO2 content of 64-66 per cent and Al2O3 of 24-26 per cent, against 52-56 per cent and 12-16 per cent for E-glass, while NE-glass was disclosed with density of 2.3 g/cm3 against 2.6 for E-glass and maximum elongation of 4.8 per cent. The published values were explicitly examples rather than guaranteed standards, but they showed that the company was willing to put concrete technical deltas into the public record. [T-glass](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/business/electronicmaterials/t-glass.htm), [NE-glass](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/business/electronicmaterials/ne-glass.htm)

## The Special-Glass Roadmap

Nittobo's public roadmap also went further than generic phrases about next-generation glass. The medium-term plan said the company would strengthen marketing and R&D for next-generation Special Glass labelled NEZ, V and DXII and would proceed to mass production after identifying customer needs. The 2025 integrated report's 5G/6G technology roadmap further identified Vlex as the low-CTE, low-loss requirement beyond today's T-glass. [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm), [Integrated Report 2025](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/pdf/Nittobo_Integrated-Report_2025.pdf)

The integrated report also described the current generation in unusually concrete terms. NE-glass was said to have become the de facto standard for low-dielectric glass and to be used in the motherboards of switches required for high-speed communication between chips in AI servers. T-glass was described as essential for semiconductor package substrates as packages became larger and more prone to warping. [Integrated Report 2025](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/pdf/Nittobo_Integrated-Report_2025.pdf)

The same report also embedded those materials in a timed roadmap rather than leaving them as static product names. It linked NE to older 25 Gbps and 50 Gbps lanes, NER to 100 Gbps-class switching, NEZ to still lower-loss future steps, and T and Vlex to the rising low-CTE needs of semiconductor package substrates as AI servers and network equipment moved up the bandwidth curve. [Integrated Report 2025](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/pdf/Nittobo_Integrated-Report_2025.pdf)

## Budget and Process Commitment

The company attached real money to that roadmap. In the May 2026 presentation, Nittobo raised the four-year R&D envelope for FY2024-2027 to approximately ¥16 billion and forecast ¥4.6 billion of R&D expense for the year ending 31 March 2027. That was not frontier-science spending on the scale of a giant chemical conglomerate, but it was material for a focused specialty materials producer of Nittobo's size. [FY2026 results presentation](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym3/202886/00.pdf), [FY2026 financial results](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym2/202884/00.pdf)

The correct conclusion from the primary materials was therefore narrower but stronger than the earlier patent-heavy narrative. Nittobo did not publicly disclose precise formulas or a detailed patent ledger in its English IR materials. It did disclose the property targets, the organisational structure, the budget trajectory and the named product roadmap that together explained how Special Glass moved from a long-running R&D theme into a commercial bottleneck of the AI hardware supply chain.

Nittobo's own October 2025 TPCA show release gave the outward-facing commercial expression of that work. The company said it would showcase low-CTE glass, low-DK glass and ultra-thin glass cloth developed with proprietary technology. That was not a patent database, but it was evidence that R&D outputs were already being packaged as a family of next-generation products for direct presentation to the PCB market before the frozen date. [TPCA Show Taipei 2025 release](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/news/pdf/20251008_newsrelease.pdf)

The medium-term plan also tied that work directly to organisational behaviour. By integrating development, manufacturing and sales within each business division while retaining a central technology function, Nittobo was effectively saying that its edge would come not only from chemistry but from how quickly it could move a material from laboratory concept to qualified production and then into customer-facing specification work. [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm)

chapters.title: AI server PCB demand cyclicality, competitive intensity, FX, geopolitical, governance
chapters.body:
## Demand Cyclicality: The Risk the Company Itself Flagged

Nittobo's own risk page was more explicit than the earlier dossier about the source of demand volatility. It said the Electronic Materials Business Division handled glass fiber yarns and cloth for IT-related printed circuit boards and semiconductor package substrates, and warned that demand for these products could fluctuate significantly with global economic trends, trade and tariff policies, geopolitical factors and downstream customer demand. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

That formulation was worth taking seriously because it came from the issuer rather than from an outside analyst. The Special Glass boom had high switching costs and long qualification cycles, but the company still saw meaningful earnings sensitivity to the broader electronics cycle.

## Competition, Substitution and the End of the Easy Narrative

The official risk language also undercut any simplistic only-supplier story. Nittobo said its technological capabilities were a source of sustainable growth, especially in electronic materials, but warned that intensified competition from domestic and foreign competitors, the development of alternative materials for glass fiber, or delays in new technology and product development could materially affect results and financial condition. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

The integrated report sharpened that point by saying Chinese and Taiwanese companies were aggressively catching up in Special Glass even as Nittobo believed it retained an overwhelming competitive advantage in low-thermal-expansion glass quality and production capacity. The risk, in other words, was not that competition did not exist; it was that the company had to keep investing ahead of it. [Integrated Report 2025](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/pdf/Nittobo_Integrated-Report_2025.pdf)

## Energy, FX and Raw Materials

The company's risk page gave three operational exposures in plain terms. First, glass fiber and glass wool production consumed LNG and electricity, leaving earnings sensitive to energy price swings. Second, the group produced in Japan, Taiwan, the U.S. and China and sold globally, so yen appreciation hurt export competitiveness while yen depreciation raised imported raw-material costs. Third, raw materials could become expensive or hard to procure because of supplier issues, macro conditions, geopolitical shocks or broader supply-chain disruption. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

Those were not generic industrial-company boilerplate. They mapped directly onto the business Nittobo had become: a high-temperature materials producer operating across Asia and North America while committing to large capital projects in Special Glass.

## Capital Investment Risk

The frozen-window numbers made this risk concrete. Nittobo forecast ¥45.0 billion of capital investment for the year ending 31 March 2027, while the medium-term plan had already been revised to approximately ¥120 billion of four-year capital investment. The company's own risk disclosure warned that large investments or periodic large-scale repairs could hurt performance if demand forecasts changed materially or if target productivity and capacity were not achieved. [FY2026 financial results](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym2/202884/00.pdf), [FY2026 results presentation](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym3/202886/00.pdf), [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

The METI-approved Fukushima supply-security project showed why this mattered. The project involved about ¥72 billion of required funding for low-thermal-expansion glass cloth capacity in Fukushima City. That was a strategic asset if AI-server and advanced-logic demand persisted, but it was also a very large commitment to one technical lane. [METI approval summary](https://www.meti.go.jp/policy/economy/economic_security/semicon/nintei_anpohandoutai_keikaku_27.pdf)

## Product Liability and Upstream Position

One of the more important operational passages in the risk page was the one most older summaries omitted. Nittobo said its glass fiber products sat upstream in the supply chain and that defects in those products could therefore create widespread downstream impact. In medical, it separately highlighted the challenge of stable quality in plant-derived raw materials and the need for group-wide quality control from antisera production in the U.S. to final manufacturing in Japan. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

That was the practical meaning of being a specialty materials supplier rather than a brand assembler: a single quality failure could travel much further than one missed shipment.

The risk-management architecture itself was also spelled out. Nittobo said it had established a basic risk-management policy in its Rules for Risk Management and operated a Risk Management Committee chaired by the Representative and Chief Executive Officer. The language was corporate, but the structure mattered because so many of the company's key risks - energy, raw materials, production outages, information security and asbestos litigation - sat across multiple divisions rather than within one plant or one end market. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

The risk page also began, tellingly, with the medium-term plan itself. Nittobo said the FY2024-2027 plan had been built on information and analysis considered appropriate at the time, but remained exposed to uncertainty and the possibility that expected results would not be achieved because of changes in the business environment. That admission mattered because by May 2026 the company had already enlarged the plan; the upside case and the planning-risk case had grown together. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm), [FY2026 results presentation](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym3/202886/00.pdf)

## Litigation, Disaster and Climate

The litigation disclosure was also specific. As of the end of the then-current consolidated fiscal year, Nittobo said the government and several dozen companies including Nittobo were defendants in damages suits brought by construction workers and bereaved families over former asbestos handling. The company stated that 32 lawsuits were pending across district and high courts in Sapporo, Sendai, Mito, Saitama, Tokyo, Yokohama, Chiba, Nagoya, Osaka, Kyoto, Hiroshima, Takamatsu, Fukuoka and Kumamoto. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

Disaster and climate risks were described in similarly operational terms. The company warned that major earthquakes, fires or interruptions to power, fuel or water could impair production, and said reinforced domestic and international climate-related regulation could affect production and sales activity or public trust. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

Nittobo also stressed the preventative side of those risks. It said it carried out BCP training and earthquake and fire drills regularly, while pursuing carbon-neutrality goals for FY2050 and using low-carbon or decarbonization technologies to cut emissions and improve productivity. The point was not that the company could neutralize these risks, but that the issuer itself treated them as operating issues, not as abstract ESG language. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

## Overseas Exposure

Finally, the group said explicitly that it had subsidiaries in Taiwan, the U.S. and China and that results could be affected by changes in politics, regulation, tax, social conditions, conflicts, disasters or infectious disease in those markets. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

The page then widened the tail-risk set beyond the market narrative. It warned about information-security failures, intellectual-property disputes, retirement-benefit assumptions, declines in the value of investment securities, and business disruption from infectious disease. None of those was the central thesis risk, but together they showed that the official risk register was much broader than a one-variable bet on AI-server demand. [Business risks](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/risk.htm)

The correct risk summary, then, was not just that AI demand might slow. It was that Nittobo had become a strategically valuable upstream materials supplier whose earnings now depended on executing a large, energy-intensive, internationally exposed capacity program while maintaining technical leadership in a niche that competitors were trying to enter.

## The Capacity Build-Out in Motion

The most usable forward numbers inside the frozen window came from the 12 May 2026 full-year report. For the year ending 31 March 2027, Nittobo forecast net sales of ¥137.0 billion, operating profit of ¥26.0 billion, EBITDA of ¥37.6 billion, capital investment of ¥45.0 billion and R&D spending of ¥4.6 billion. The same presentation showed Electronic Materials alone forecast at ¥77.0 billion of sales and ¥26.0 billion of operating profit. [FY2026 financial results](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym2/202884/00.pdf), [FY2026 results presentation](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym3/202886/00.pdf)

Those forecasts mattered because they showed management still assuming another year of heavy Special Glass demand rather than a normalization back toward pre-AI mix.

## A Revised Medium-Term Horizon

Nittobo also raised its FY2027 medium-term targets in May 2026 to ¥155.0 billion of net sales, ¥36.0 billion of operating profit and ¥51.0 billion of EBITDA, with approximately ¥120 billion of four-year capital investment and approximately ¥16 billion of four-year R&D spend. That was a far stronger planning stance than the original FY2024-2027 framework, which had targeted ¥135 billion, ¥20 billion and approximately ¥80 billion respectively. [FY2026 results presentation](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym3/202886/00.pdf), [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm)

## Where the Company Itself Expected Demand to Come From

The company was explicit about the demand sources it expected to stay firm. The FY2027 outlook said it expected strong demand for Special Glass used in electronic materials, particularly for servers at data centers, network equipment and semiconductor package substrates. The segment outlook added that demand for low-thermal-expansion glass for server and edge-device semiconductor package substrates should increase significantly, while robust demand for low-dielectric glass for data centers should continue. [FY2026 financial results](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym2/202884/00.pdf), [FY2026 results presentation](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym3/202886/00.pdf)

That was the important correction to the older, more speculative customer-concentration passages. Nittobo's official outlook stayed application-led - data centers, network gear, package substrates - rather than naming individual laminator or hyperscaler customers.

The segment commentary added more operational colour. For Electronic Materials, management expected significant growth in low-thermal-expansion glass for server and edge-device semiconductor package substrates, both thick and thin, and said robust demand for NE-glass and NER-glass for data centers should continue. For the rest of the group, the stated objectives were more incremental: opening new customers and collaborating with major overseas players in Medical, trying to lift sales in Electrical and Electronics in Composite Materials, and relying on new product launches or housing recovery in Materials Solution and Insulation. [FY2026 results presentation](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym3/202886/00.pdf)

## Technology Migration and the Company's Own Roadmap

Nittobo's integrated report did not pretend today's Special Glass families were the end-state. The medium-term plan named next-generation Special Glass programmes NEZ, V and DXII, while the integrated report's technology roadmap added Vlex as the low-CTE, low-loss target beyond today's T-glass and showed co-packaged optics on the longer-term data-centre architecture map. [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm), [Integrated Report 2025](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/pdf/Nittobo_Integrated-Report_2025.pdf)

Even so, the same primary materials still placed conventional glass-reinforced boards and substrates at the centre of the company's near-term planning. Management was forecasting another year of rising sales and profit while investing heavily in glass cloth capacity, not signaling that optical substitution was about to displace the core product set.

The medium-term plan said the Electronic Materials division would respond by moving ahead with further investment to expand Special Glass production in Japan and overseas, while strengthening marketing and R&D for NEZ, V and DXII. In other words, the company's own answer to migration risk was not retrenchment but a faster push into the next specifications. [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm)

The plan's published logic also remained recognisably sequential. Management said it would first harvest the fruits of earlier investment in Special Glass and medical, then build additional revenue pillars for the next 100 years beyond 2030. That ordering mattered because it meant the company was not presenting 2026-2030 as a period of wholesale diversification away from Special Glass; it was presenting it as a period in which Special Glass cash generation would fund the search for whatever came next. [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm)

## What Had to Go Right Through 2030

For Nittobo to validate the enlarged plan, three things had to hold. The first was sustained demand for low-thermal-expansion and low-dielectric Special Glass in servers, switches and semiconductor package substrates. The second was execution: the company had to translate a very large capex program into qualified capacity on time. The third was technical succession: NE had to migrate to NER and NEZ on the low-loss side, while T had to move toward V and Vlex on the low-CTE side. [Integrated Report 2025](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/pdf/Nittobo_Integrated-Report_2025.pdf), [Medium-Term Management Plan](https://www.nittobo.co.jp/eng/ir/keiei/chukei.htm), [FY2026 results presentation](https://ssl4.eir-parts.net/doc/3110/ir_material_for_fiscal_ym3/202886/00.pdf)

Nittobo's own disclosures therefore supported a bullish but disciplined forward view. The company had already raised its plan, backed it with capex and R&D, and published a product roadmap beyond the current generation. The unresolved question was not whether management saw a bigger market. It was whether the company could enlarge its physical and technical lead faster than competitors could narrow it.

## C. Business Divisions

1. **Electronic Materials** — Special Glass and related yarn and cloth for printed wiring boards, AI-server motherboards, network switches and semiconductor package substrates.
2. **Medical** — In-vitro diagnostic reagents with integrated production from raw materials to finished products.
3. **Composite Materials** — Glass fiber as plastic reinforcing material for FRP and FRTP applications.
4. **Materials Solution** — Glass fiber for industrial materials, chemical products and the legacy textile business.
5. **Insulation Materials** — Glass wool and related insulation products, mainly through Paramount Glass Manufacturing.

---

## D. Disclosed End Markets

| Application area | What Nittobo disclosed |
|---|---|
| AI servers and network switches | Low-dielectric motherboards using Special Glass |
| Semiconductor package substrates | Low-CTE packages for CPUs, GPUs, ASICs, DRAM and NAND |
| Data-center communications | NE-glass, NER-glass and successor low-loss products |
| Buildings and housing | Glass wool insulation |
| Medical diagnostics | In-vitro diagnostic reagents |

Public Nittobo disclosures reviewed through 23 May 2026 did not publish a company-verified list of laminate-company customers by name.

---

## E. Competitive Framing in Primary Sources

Nittobo's primary disclosures did not provide a verified named-peer table with market shares. They did say, however, that Chinese and Taiwanese companies were aggressively catching up in Special Glass, that Nittobo retained an overwhelming competitive advantage in quality and production capacity for low-thermal-expansion glass, and that competition from domestic and foreign rivals and alternative materials remained a disclosed business risk.
